mcqs.question: What should you name first when explaining how a retry storm develops, before proposing a fix?
options: The exact version number of the HTTP client library involved
The total number of servers in the downstream dependency's cluster
Which cloud provider hosts the dependency
The feedback loop — failure causes retries, retries cause more failure, more failure causes more retries
mcqs.explanation: Naming the self-reinforcing loop explains why the fix (backoff and jitter) actually works, rather than just stating a remedy. The client library version, cluster size, and hosting provider aren't what makes a retry storm self-reinforcing.

mcqs.question: 10,000 clients use a fixed 5-second timeout with immediate retry on failure. A dependency has a 2-second blip. What happens?
options: All 10,000 requests fail together and retry at the same instant, multiplying load exactly when the dependency is least able to absorb it
The requests fail gradually over several minutes, giving the dependency time to recover
Only the first 100 clients experience the failure; the rest are unaffected
The fixed timeout prevents any requests from failing during a 2-second blip
mcqs.explanation: Because all clients share the same fixed timeout and no jitter, they fail and retry in near-perfect synchrony, concentrating load into a spike rather than spreading it out. Nothing here staggers the failures gradually, limits impact to a subset of clients, or prevents failures during the blip.

mcqs.question: What do backoff-with-jitter and circuit breakers cost the failing request path, in exchange for preventing a retry storm?
options: They guarantee every request eventually succeeds, no matter how long the outage lasts
They eliminate the need for any monitoring on the dependency
They add latency — requests wait longer before retrying, and sometimes fail fast instead of eventually succeeding
They require rewriting the dependency's own service code
mcqs.explanation: The real cost is added latency and, once a breaker opens, deliberately failing fast rather than continuing to retry — a worthwhile trade to avoid amplifying an outage. Neither mechanism guarantees eventual success, removes the need for monitoring, or requires changes to the dependency itself.

mcqs.question: During a partial outage, should every client retry the same number of times?
options: No — retries should decrease or stop for lower-priority callers first, so critical traffic gets whatever retry budget remains
Yes, uniform retry counts are always the fairest approach for every caller
No, only the client that first detected the failure should be allowed to retry
Yes, but only if all callers belong to the same team
mcqs.explanation: Prioritizing retries lets critical traffic, like a checkout request, keep more of the limited retry budget than lower-priority background work during a partial outage. Uniform treatment ignores that not all traffic matters equally, restricting retries to a single detecting client doesn't reflect how distributed callers actually operate, and team ownership is irrelevant to request priority.
